CLASS 29 · SIGHT WORDS

Learn the sight words, one card at a time.

Fifty-two sight word lessons, five minutes each: look at the card, say the word, play one tiny game and spot it in a real book. Start with a, the, I and you, then the action words, the colours and the little words that join sentences together.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

A — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “a” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I have a dog.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It comes before a thing and tells us there is just one.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “a” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: one small curl with a short stem, easy to find even in small print.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “a” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say a soft uh, like the start of about: quick and light. Save the letter name ay for singing the alphabet.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I have a dog.” Then try “She ate a red apple.” Where to spot it: the front of almost every picture-book sentence, right before a thing.

Try this game

Put a ball, a toy and a spoon in a bag. Pull them out one at a time and say a ball, a toy, a spoon.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “a” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Keep it to five minutes, and add “a” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the A flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

The — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “the” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“The cat sat on the mat.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It points at the one particular thing we mean.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “the” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: three letters marching left to right: a tall t, a tall h and a little e.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “the” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Start with th, tongue tip resting lightly between your teeth, then a quick uh. Before a vowel sound it often turns into thee, as in the apple.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “The cat sat on the mat.” Then try “Please close the door.” Where to spot it: titles like The Zoo and The End, and almost every line of a story.

Try this game

Ask for things by name: pass me the cup, hand me the spoon. Each time, your child holds up the card when they hear the.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “the” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Do not drill “the” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the The flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

I — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “I” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I like cake.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It is the word a person uses when they talk about themselves.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “I” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a single tall stick, like a person standing straight.
  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.
  3. Play the game below, say “I” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say it like the letter name, eye. It rhymes with fly and sky.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I like cake.” Then try “I can see a bird.” Where to spot it: the start of a sentence, whenever someone talks about themselves.

Try this game

Say I like, I can and I see, and let your child finish each one. Tap your chest every time you say I.

Understanding check

Ask your child to say one real sentence about themselves or someone nearby that uses “I”. A sentence they made up is the best proof.

Parent tips

If “I” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

This lesson pairs with the I flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

You — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “you” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I see you.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It means the person we are talking to.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “you” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: three round shapes that look like they are saying yoo.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “you” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say yoo, starting with the y of yes. It rhymes with too and blue.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I see you.” Then try “Thank you for the hug.” Where to spot it: thank you notes, birthday songs and every I love you.

Try this game

Point at someone and say you, then point at yourself and say me. Swap roles and let your child do the pointing.

Understanding check

Ask your child to say one real sentence about themselves or someone nearby that uses “you”. A sentence they made up is the best proof.

Parent tips

Keep it to five minutes, and add “you” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the You flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Me — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “me” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Look at me.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It is the word for ourselves when something is done to us or for us.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “me” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: two little humps next to a letter e, like a pair of hills.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “me” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say mee, with a long ee. It rhymes with see and tree.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Look at me.” Then try “Can you help me?” Where to spot it: give it to me, help me, me too.

Try this game

Give yourself a hug and say me, then hug a teddy and say you. Let your child do both parts.

Understanding check

Ask your child to say one real sentence about themselves or someone nearby that uses “me”. A sentence they made up is the best proof.

Parent tips

Do not drill “me” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the Me flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

My — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “my” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“This is my bed.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells us who owns something.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “my” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: an m followed by a y with a tail that drops below the line.
  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.
  3. Play the game below, say “my” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say my so it rhymes with fly. Say it with a smile.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “This is my bed.” Then try “My ball is red.” Where to spot it: labels on cubbies, name tags and my first book.

Try this game

Collect three of your child's things and say my cup, my hat, my book. Let your child say it as you hand each one over.

Understanding check

Ask your child to say one real sentence about themselves or someone nearby that uses “my”. A sentence they made up is the best proof.

Parent tips

If “my” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

This lesson pairs with the My flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

We — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “we” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“We can play.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It means me and other people together.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “we” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a w that looks like two valleys, followed by a little e.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “we” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say wee, with lips rounded first for the w. It rhymes with me and see.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “We can play.” Then try “We are a team.” Where to spot it: storybook friends and family plans, such as we are going.

Try this game

Hold hands in a circle and say We can clap, We can hop, We can spin. Do each action as you say it.

Understanding check

Ask your child to say one real sentence about themselves or someone nearby that uses “we”. A sentence they made up is the best proof.

Parent tips

Keep it to five minutes, and add “we” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the We flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

It — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “it” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I see it.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It stands in for a thing we already mentioned.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “it” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a tall i sitting next to a tall t, as if the two are holding hands.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “it” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say a short i then a crisp t: it, like sit and bit.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I see it.” Then try “It is a ball.” Where to spot it: pointing at something and saying what it is.

Try this game

Hide a toy, then say Where is it? When your child finds it, they say I see it. Take turns hiding.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “it” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Do not drill “it” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the It flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Is — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “is” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“The sun is hot.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells us what something or someone is like.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “is” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a small i with a curvy s that hisses at the end.
  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.
  3. Play the game below, say “is” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say a short i and end with a buzzing z: iz. It is not iss.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “The sun is hot.” Then try “He is happy.” Where to spot it: sentences about how things are, like the cat is big.

Try this game

Say a thing and add a word: The ball is red. The sky is blue. Your child adds the next is sentence.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “is” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

If “is” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

This lesson pairs with the Is flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Am — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “am” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I am six.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It always goes with I when we say who we are.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “am” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: two arches beside a rounded letter a.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “am” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Open your mouth for the short a, then close your lips for m: am, like ham.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I am six.” Then try “I am happy.” Where to spot it: I am sentences, such as I am hungry or I am a helper.

Try this game

Take turns finishing I am... with a feeling or an action. Do the matching face or motion.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “am” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Keep it to five minutes, and add “am” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the Am flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Are — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “are” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“You are kind.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells us what two or more people or things are like.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “are” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: an a and an r followed by a silent e at the end.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “are” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say ar like the letter R. It rhymes with car and star.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “You are kind.” Then try “We are friends.” Where to spot it: sentences about groups, such as we are, they are and you are.

Try this game

Call out two things and say they are: The socks are warm. The shoes are by the door. Let your child add one.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “are” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Do not drill “are” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the Are flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Be — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “be” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I want to be a pilot.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It is the word we use for who we are and who we want to be.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “be” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a b with its round belly on the right, followed by a little e.
  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.
  3. Play the game below, say “be” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Pop your lips for b, then hold a long ee: bee, like the insect.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I want to be a pilot.” Then try “Be kind.” Where to spot it: wishes and instructions, such as be careful and be quiet.

Try this game

Ask What do you want to be? and let your child answer with I want to be... Then be that thing for a moment.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “be” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

If “be” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

This lesson pairs with the Be flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Can — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “can” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I can jump.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells us what someone is able to do.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “can” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a round c, an a and an n, all friends in a row.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “can” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say a short a, then n: can, like fan and man.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I can jump.” Then try “Can you help me?” Where to spot it: proud claims and polite questions, such as I can do it.

Try this game

Take turns saying I can and then doing a skill: I can hop, I can clap, I can wink.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “can” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Keep it to five minutes, and add “can” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the Can flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

And — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “and” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Cats and dogs play.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It joins two or more things together.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “and” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: an a, an n and a d standing in a row, with a tall d to finish.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “and” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say each sound clearly, a-n-d, and end with a light d. In fast talking it shrinks to un.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Cats and dogs play.” Then try “I like red and blue.” Where to spot it: lists, such as bread and butter, mom and dad.

Try this game

Name two things you see, then link them with and: socks and shoes, up and down. Let your child add a third.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “and” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Do not drill “and” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the And flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

In — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “in” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“The ball is in the box.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells us something is inside something else.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “in” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a tall i next to a hill-shaped n, like a person standing beside a hill.
  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.
  3. Play the game below, say “in” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say a short i then n: in, like pin and win.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “The ball is in the box.” Then try “Put it in the bag.” Where to spot it: boxes, cups, pockets and anywhere something can hide inside.

Try this game

Put a toy in a box, a sock in a shoe, a spoon in a cup. Say in each time and let your child do the next one.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “in” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

If “in” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

This lesson pairs with the In flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

To — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “to” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Give it to me.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It shows direction or a person who receives.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “to” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a t with a crossbar followed by a round o.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “to” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say too. It rhymes with do and who, though the spelling is different.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Give it to me.” Then try “We go to the park.” Where to spot it: going places and giving things, such as to the store and to you.

Try this game

Pass a toy from hand to hand and say I give it to you. Then walk to the door and say We go to the door.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “to” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Keep it to five minutes, and add “to” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the To flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

Up — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “up” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Look up at the sky.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It means toward a higher place.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “up” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a u that opens upward and a p with its stem going down.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “up” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say a short u then p: up, like cup and pup.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Look up at the sky.” Then try “Please stand up.” Where to spot it: stairs, ladders and climbing, and stand-up commands.

Try this game

Reach your hands up and say up. Say Hands up! and stretch like a tree. Then lower them and say down.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “up” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Do not drill “up” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the Up flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

Down — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “down” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Sit down, please.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It means toward a lower place.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “down” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a d with its belly, then an o and a w that looks like two valleys.
  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.
  3. Play the game below, say “down” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say d, then ow as in cow: down, like town and crown.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Sit down, please.” Then try “The ball rolled down the hill.” Where to spot it: slides, stairs and sit-down instructions.

Try this game

Stand on a low step and say down as you step off. Do it again with a doll or a toy.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “down” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

If “down” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

This lesson pairs with the Down flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

Go — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “go” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“We can go now.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It means to move or begin.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “go” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a round g next to a round o, like two wheels.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “go” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say go with a long o, like no and toe.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “We can go now.” Then try “Go to sleep.” Where to spot it: traffic lights, races and ready, set, go.

Try this game

Stand at one end of the room. Say ready, set, go and walk to the other end. Repeat with a new action.

Understanding check

Say “go” and ask your child to show you with their body, then to read the card back to you without help.

This lesson pairs with the Here flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Where — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “where” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Where is my hat?”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It is the word we use to ask about a place.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “where” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a w, an h, an e, an r and an e.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “where” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say wair, like chair and bear. The h is silent.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Where is my hat?” Then try “Where are you?” Where to spot it: questions and searches, such as where is the cat.

Try this game

Hide a toy and ask Where is it? Say where each time you ask.

Understanding check

Ask your child to show “where” by pointing or moving, then to read the card without help.

Parent tips

Do not drill “where” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the Where flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Away — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “away” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Go away.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It means off from here, to somewhere else.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “away” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: an a, a w, an a and a y that make a path.
  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.
  3. Play the game below, say “away” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say it in two chunks: uh-way. The first part is soft.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Go away.” Then try “The bird flew away.” Where to spot it: goodbyes, such as go away and put it away.

Try this game

Walk away from your child and say I walk away. Then walk back and say I came back.

Understanding check

Ask your child to show “away” by pointing or moving, then to read the card without help.

Parent tips

If “away” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

This lesson pairs with the Away flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

At — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “at” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“Look at me.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells us where or when.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “at” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a tiny a with a t that has a crossbar.
  2. On the drawing canvas, let your child trace over the word with a finger or the pencil, then circle any letter they already know.
  3. Play the game below, say “at” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say a short a: at, like cat and hat.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “Look at me.” Then try “I am at home.” Where to spot it: places and times, such as at school and at six.

Try this game

Say at the door, at the table, at the window and stand there each time.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “at” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Keep it to five minutes, and add “at” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

This lesson pairs with the At flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SIGHT WORDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

By — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “by” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“The dog sat by me.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It means near or next to.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “by” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: a b with a belly and a y with a tail.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “by” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say by like the word bye. It rhymes with fly.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “The dog sat by me.” Then try “I stand by the door.” Where to spot it: being near someone or something, such as by the tree.

Try this game

Stand by the chair, by the table and by the door. Say by each time.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “by” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Parent tips

Do not drill “by” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

This lesson pairs with the By flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sight Words (Class 29).

Say for, like four and door.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “This is for you.” Then try “I made it for mom.” Where to spot it: gifts and cards, such as for you.

Hand an item to someone and say This is for you. Swap roles.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “for” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

If “for” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

Not — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “not” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I do not like peas.”) and finish with one small game.

Say a short o: not, like hot and pot.

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “not” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Say a short u: but, like cut and nut.

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “but” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “all” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

If “all” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

Said — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “said” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“She said hello.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells that someone spoke.

How to teach it

  3. Play the game below, say “said” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say sed, like bed and red. It does not rhyme with paid.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “She said hello.” Then try “I said yes.” Where to spot it: speech in stories, such as he said.

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “said” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.

Keep it to five minutes, and add “said” to the card pile only when the words your child already knows feel easy.

Ate — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Five minutes, one card: say “ate” clearly, use it in a real sentence (“I ate a plum.”) and finish with one small game.

What it means

It tells that someone already had a meal.

How to teach it

  1. Hold up the card and read “ate” slowly, sliding a finger under it. Point out its shape: an a, a t and a silent e.
  2. Ask your child to find the first letter on the canvas and draw a ring around it, then say the whole word.
  3. Play the game below, say “ate” one last time and stop while it is still fun.

How to say it

Say ayt, like late and gate. It sounds like eight.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I ate a plum.” Then try “She ate lunch.” Where to spot it: meals and stories about food, such as the bear ate.

Try this game

Ask What did you eat? and say I ate... Take turns.

Understanding check

Say “ate” and ask your child to show you with their body, then to read the card back to you without help.

Parent tips

Do not drill “ate” on its own for long. Slip it into the books you read today and let the story do the practicing.

Did — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

  2. Cover the word with a hand and ask your child to say it from memory. Draw a big tick on the canvas when they get it.

How to say it

Say a short i: did, like kid and lid.

Where to use it

Say it in a real sentence: “I did it.” Then try “What did you do?” Where to spot it: questions and proud claims, such as did you.

Try this game

Understanding check

Say “did” and ask your child to show you with their body, then to read the card back to you without help.

Parent tips

If “did” slips away overnight, that is normal. Bring it back the next day with the same game and a smile.

Tomorrow, show the card and say nothing. If your child reads “could” at once, it has arrived; if not, play the game again the day after.
